archetype.name: Dual-Threat (scramble-first)
archetype.definition: Maye is a rhythm passer from the pocket who does his rushing damage by escaping and scrambling rather than on called runs. He holds the ball to let routes and running lanes develop.

report.headline: Turnovers, not accuracy, are sinking a QB who's still throwing it well
report.take:
Maye arrived in 2026 off a season that ranked third in the league in EPA per play (0.315), third in CPOE (10.8) and fourth in success rate. That is the baseline that matters. Four games in, his passing EPA per dropback sits at -0.071, 29th of 42. The easy read is a sophomore-to-third-year collapse. The dossier doesn't support that read. His bad-throw rate of 6% ranks third among 32 charted passers, and his CPOE is still positive. His ball is going where he wants it to. What has broken is the outcome column: 7 interceptions on 117 attempts, a 6% rate that ranks 39th, plus 2 lost fumbles.

The passing tree tells the story. Downfield he has been good. He's at +0.28 EPA on intermediate throws and +0.388 on deep shots, even with 3 deep picks included. The failures sit at the shallow end. Throws behind the line have produced -0.425 EPA with a CPOE of -16.5 on 24 attempts, and Rhamondre Stevenson's -0.281 EPA per target on 17 looks is the clearest symptom. Short throws are completing at 75% (+10.6 CPOE) yet net out to zero EPA because 2 of them went the other way. Third down (-0.327) and the red zone (-0.482) are where the giveaways have hurt most, and 3 of the 7 picks came in close fourth quarters.

Context matters too. Three of his four opponents rank 3rd, 13th and 7th in defensive EPA today. The one soft defense, Buffalo at 29th, got a 269-yard, 3-TD, +11 EPA game out of him. The receiver room is also shifting under him. A.J. Brown played one game before going to IR. Mack Hollins, his most efficient target at 0.636 EPA per target, is now questionable with a calf injury.

What stays constant is the scrambling. He has 14 scrambles for 136 yards and 11 first downs, worth 1.155 EPA apiece. That is why he ranks second among QBs in rushing yards despite designed runs going nowhere (1 yard per carry on 5 tries). The flip side is the same as in prior seasons: a 3.04-second time to throw and a 39% pressure-to-sack rate. That cost is real, but the scrambles more than pay for it. The interception rate is the part most likely to come down.

strengths.title: Scrambles that move the chains
strengths.body: When the pocket breaks down he turns dropbacks into first downs: 11 of his 14 scrambles moved the sticks, at more than a full expected point each. It is the reason he ranks second at the position in rushing yards while called runs have been stuffed 40% of the time. He has rushed for 421 and 450 yards the last two seasons, so this is a durable part of his game rather than a hot streak.

strengths.title: Ball placement is still intact
strengths.body: His bad-throw rate ranks third among charted passers. That is better than his 2024 (15.4%) and 2025 (13.2%) marks, and it argues the interceptions are more about decisions and tipped or contested balls than lost accuracy. Paired with a positive CPOE, it points to a passer whose underlying skill hasn't eroded from last year's top-three season.

strengths.title: Downfield throws are paying off
strengths.body: Beyond 10 air yards he has been efficient: +0.28 EPA on 32 intermediate attempts and +0.388 on 17 deep shots. His intended air yards (9.54) match last year's 9.1 aDOT, so he hasn't gotten timid. Deep samples this small swing hard, but the efficiency fits who he was in 2025.

concerns.title: Interceptions in the worst spots
concerns.body: A 6% interception rate is roughly triple what a passer of his 2025 quality should carry. Last year he threw 8 picks across 17 games; this year it's 7 in 4. Three came on deep shots and three in close fourth quarters, so the damage is concentrated in high-leverage moments. The rate should fall toward his career norm, but the late-game decision-making is the part to keep watching.

concerns.title: The screen and checkdown game is broken
concerns.body: Throws behind the line are producing -0.425 EPA on 24 attempts with a CPOE of -16.5. Stevenson is at -0.281 EPA per target. This is more a scheme and personnel failure than a Maye flaw: those plays depend on blocking and run-after-catch from a backfield on an offense ranked 24th in rushing EPA. Until it improves, the easy completions that should steady drives aren't there.

concerns.title: Sacks are the price of extending plays
concerns.body: His pressure-to-sack rate of 39.1% ranks 30th of 32, and his time to throw is 3.04 seconds. He ran a 40.5% rate as a rookie and 35.6% last year, so this is who he is rather than a new problem. It's a trade, since the same holding-on produces those scrambles. It still bites on third down, where he is at -0.327 EPA and converting 31.4% with 7.2 yards to go on average.

trend.note: He was steady but turnover-marred against strong defenses in Weeks 1-2, then bottomed out at -14.2 EPA in the Jacksonville blowout. He bounced back to +11 EPA and 26.2 PPR points at Buffalo, but that came against the 29th-ranked defense. That makes Week 4 a hint of recovery, not proof of one.

nextGame.headline: Top-three pass defense that gets home tests his sack habit
nextGame.body:
Las Vegas brings the second-best defense by EPA and the third-best pass defense. It also gets hits on the quarterback at the second-highest rate in the league and ranks fifth in sack rate. That collides with the most fragile part of Maye's profile, his tendency to take sacks while extending plays. The Raiders also take away the deep ball, ranking fifth in deep EPA allowed, which is where his passing has been most productive. The opening is underneath. Their short-pass defense ranks 24th, and Maye's short completions have been accurate (+10.6 CPOE). The question is whether he can string those together without the turnovers that have erased them. The other opening is scrambling: Vegas ranks 27th in explosive runs allowed, and a rush that gets upfield can leave lanes behind it.

Availability leans against him. Mack Hollins, his most efficient target, is questionable with a calf injury, and the team is unsure he can practice for a couple of days. A.J. Brown is on IR until around November 1, and tight end Eli Raridon is also questionable. Without Hollins the target pool tilts further toward Doubs, Douglas, Henry and a backfield producing negative EPA per target. On the other side, Raiders guard Jackson Powers-Johnson (98% of snaps) is listed out, and their receiver group is thinned by Jack Bech's IR stint and Jalen Nailor's concussion. That should help New England's fifth-ranked pass defense keep the score manageable, so Maye isn't forced into the trailing-by-9+ situations where he has been at -0.437 EPA.

keyMatchups.title: Raiders' pass rush vs his sack rate
keyMatchups.body: Vegas hits quarterbacks at a 22.4% rate, second in the league, and Maye converts pressure into sacks 39% of the time. Expect multiple sacks unless the ball comes out faster than his 3.04-second average. How often he escapes for scrambles instead of going down is the swing of his day.

keyMatchups.title: Underneath is open, deep is not
keyMatchups.body: Las Vegas allows +0.134 EPA on short passes (24th) but -0.191 on deep balls (5th). The plan should be volume in the 0-9 range, where Maye completes 75% of his throws. Patient, short-heavy passing keeps the turnover risk down; forcing shots into this secondary invites more of it.

keyMatchups.title: Hollins' calf and the target tree
keyMatchups.body: Hollins has turned 19 targets into 0.636 EPA each, double anyone else in the group, while playing 65% of snaps. Losing him with Brown already out leaves Maye with fewer reliable downfield options. That would push him further toward the dump-offs that haven't worked.

nextGame.watch: Whether pressure turns into scrambles and first downs rather than sacks and forced throws, and whether Hollins is active.

restOfSeason.body:
The interception rate is the number most likely to move, and it should move in his favor. A 6% pick rate alongside a top-three bad-throw rate and positive CPOE is an outlier on four games. His 2025 season, with 8 picks over 17 games and a top-three EPA, says the decision-making is better than this. The early schedule also front-loaded good defenses. The scrambling value is sustainable, and so is the sack rate, since both have held for three seasons. A return to his 2025 level of 8.9 yards per attempt and 31 TDs is unlikely without Brown and with the screen game this broken. Something like an above-average starter's output, with weekly rushing yards in the 30s, is the reasonable middle.

The biggest lift should come around Brown's expected return near November 1, if Hollins is healthy by then too. Until then the receiving group is thin. An offense ranked 24th in rushing EPA also won't take much pressure off him, so expect uneven weeks against good pass defenses like this one and spikes against soft ones like Buffalo.
swingFactors: A.J. Brown's return from IR around Nov. 1
Hollins' calf and the depth of the receiving corps
Whether the interception rate normalizes toward his 2025 level

bets.reason: Three of New England's four games have gone under. The Raiders bring the No. 2 defense by EPA, and the Patriots' own pass defense ranks 5th against a Raiders receiver group missing Bech and possibly Nailor.
Las Vegas ranks 3rd in pass-defense EPA and 5th against deep throws, his most productive depth. His top target Hollins is questionable and Brown is on IR.
A pass rush that hits QBs at the second-highest rate will flush him often, and he turns scrambles into 1.155 EPA and first downs at a high clip. The Raiders also rank 27th in explosive runs allowed.

The market lays more than a field goal with an offense ranked 22nd in EPA against the league's No. 2 defense. Maye's turnover rate makes a margin-of-a-field-goal game more likely than a comfortable cover, even with the Raiders' line and receivers banged up.

confidence.note: Only four games, three against strong defenses, but a top-three 2025 baseline. Receiver availability (Hollins, Brown) is the main unknown.
